cues.text: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome to Stories of the Prophets.
In this episode, the story of one of the companions of our Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
For years, there was a man who stood against Islam.
At Uhud, it was his horsemen who turned the battle against the believers.
And one day, the Messenger of Allah looked at this same man, and said: what a good servant of Allah he is.
A sword of the swords of Allah.
His name was Khalid ibn al-Walid.
This is the story of how Allah guided a brave heart, and how that bravery was spent, from then on, for the sake of Allah.
Khalid was from Banu Makhzum, one of the noblest clans of Quraysh.
He grew up on horseback, and learned the sword, the spear and the bow, and how armies move, when to strike, and when to wait.
While he was still young, he was known across Arabia as a leader of horsemen.
When the believers emigrated to Madinah, Khalid rode out with Quraysh against them.
At Uhud, he commanded their cavalry.
When the archers left their hill, it was Khalid who saw the gap, rode around it, and attacked the believers from behind.
But Allah knows what is in the hearts, before their owners know it themselves.
After the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, Khalid began to think.
The books of Seerah record that he said: there was not one battle I fought against Muhammad,
except that I came away feeling that I had fought for nothing, and that he would win in the end.
His brother, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, had already become Muslim, and he wrote to Khalid: the Messenger of Allah asked me about you.
He said: where is Khalid?
A man like him cannot stay ignorant of Islam.
If he used his courage with the Muslims, it would be better for him.
In the eighth year after the Hijrah, Khalid set out for Madinah.
On the road he met Amr ibn al-As, another great leader of Quraysh, who was going for the very same reason.
The books of Seerah record that Khalid said: the Messenger of Allah kept smiling at me, until I stood before him.
I said:
I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that you are the Messenger of Allah.
He said: praise be to Allah, who has guided you.
I saw that you had a good mind, and I hoped it would lead you only to good.
Amr ibn al-As described his own moment.
He said:
I put out my hand to give my pledge, then I pulled it back.
The Prophet said: what is the matter, Amr?
I said:
I want a condition: that I am forgiven.
He said: do you not know that Islam wipes away what came before it?
This was reported by Imam Muslim.
And Allah says:
Say to those who have disbelieved that if they cease, what has previously occurred will be forgiven for them.
But if they return, then the example of the former peoples has already taken place.
Only a few months later, the Prophet sent an army of three thousand men north, towards the lands of the Romans.
Khalid went with them, not as a commander, but as a soldier.
The Prophet chose the leaders himself.
He said:
Zayd ibn Harithah is your leader.
If Zayd is killed, then Jafar.
And if Jafar is killed, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
At a place called Mutah, they found themselves facing an army far larger than any they had ever seen.
The books of Seerah speak of a hundred thousand men or more.
Some of the believers said: let us write to the Messenger of Allah, and tell him how many they are.
Then Abdullah ibn Rawahah stood and said:
O my people, what you dislike now is the very thing you came out to seek: martyrdom.
We do not fight with numbers.
We fight with this religion, with which Allah has honoured us.
The books of Seerah record this.
Zayd ibn Harithah took the flag, and fought until he was killed.
Then Jafar ibn Abi Talib, the cousin of the Prophet, took the flag, and fought until he too was killed.
Abdullah ibn Umar said:
I was in that army.
We found Jafar among the dead, and there were more than ninety wounds on his body,
from spears and arrows, and not one of them was in his back.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Then Abdullah ibn Rawahah took the flag, and he too was martyred.
And the people agreed on Khalid ibn al-Walid.
At that very hour, far away in Madinah, the Prophet stood before the people.
Anas ibn Malik said: the Prophet told the people of the deaths of Zayd, Jafar and Ibn Rawahah before the news had reached them.
He said:
Zayd took the flag, and was killed.
Then Jafar took it, and was killed.
Then Ibn Rawahah took it, and was killed.
And his eyes were full of tears.
Then he said: until a sword of the swords of Allah took the flag, and Allah gave them victory.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
From that day on, Khalid was known as Sayfullah, the Sword of Allah.
And about those who are martyred, Allah says:
And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead.
Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision, rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty.
And they receive good tidings about those who have not yet joined them,
that there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.
Khalid found himself at the head of a tired army that had lost its three leaders in one day, facing an enemy many times its size.
He said: on the day of Mutah, nine swords broke in my hand.
Nothing was left in my hand but a broad Yemeni blade.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
The historians record that when night came, Khalid changed the whole shape of the army.
He moved the right side to the left, and the left to the right.
He brought the men from the back to the front, and sent horsemen behind the hills, to ride back in the morning raising dust.
When the sun rose, the Romans saw new faces and new flags, and they thought that help had come from Madinah.
They held back.
And Khalid drew the army away, slowly and in order, and brought it home.
Bravery is not only charging forward.
Sometimes the bravest thing is to protect the people in your care.
Khalid brought almost the whole army home.
Abu Hurayrah said: we were travelling with the Messenger of Allah, and people were passing by.
He would ask: who is this?
Then Khalid passed, and he asked: who is this?
I said:
Khalid ibn al-Walid.
And he said: what a good servant of Allah is Khalid ibn al-Walid.
A sword of the swords of Allah.
This was reported by Imam at-Tirmidhi.
In the eleventh year after the Hijrah, the Messenger of Allah passed away.
Many tribes turned back from Islam, and false prophets appeared.
The most dangerous was Musaylimah the liar, in the land of al-Yamamah, with a great army behind him.
The caliph, Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, sent Khalid.
The historians record that it was one of the fiercest battles the companions ever fought,
and again and again the Muslim lines were pushed back.
The enemy fell back into a walled garden, and locked the gates.
The historians record that al-Bara ibn Malik said: throw me over the wall to them.
They lifted him on their shields, and he went over alone, fought his way to the gate, and opened it for the Muslims.
They called that place the Garden of Death.
Allah gave the Muslims victory, and Musaylimah was killed by the spear of Wahshi, the same man who had killed Hamzah at Uhud.
Wahshi had become Muslim, and he said:
I went out to Musaylimah, hoping to kill him, and make up for killing Hamzah.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Two men who had harmed the believers at Uhud, Khalid and Wahshi, now stood together in the service of Islam.
But the victory was costly.
Many who knew the Quran by heart were martyred at al-Yamamah.
Zayd ibn Thabit said:
Abu Bakr sent for me, and Umar was with him.
Abu Bakr said:
Umar came to me and said: many of the reciters of the Quran were killed on the day of al-Yamamah,
and I fear that much of the Quran will be lost.
I think you should order the Quran to be collected.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
So the Quran was gathered into one book, just as Allah had promised to guard it:
Indeed, it is We who sent down the message, the Quran, and indeed, We will be its guardian.
Then Abu Bakr sent Khalid to Syria, and there came al-Yarmuk,
where the Romans gathered one of their greatest armies, many times larger than the army of the Muslims.
The historians record that before the battle, a Roman commander named Jarajah rode out and called for Khalid.
He asked him: did Allah send a sword from the sky to your Prophet, and he gave it to you?
Khalid said: no.
We fought against the Prophet, until Allah opened my heart and I followed him.
And he called me a sword of the swords of Allah.
And Jarajah asked about Islam, became Muslim there and then, crossed over to the Muslim side, and was martyred that same day.
And Allah gave the Muslims victory at al-Yarmuk.
But perhaps the bravest thing Khalid ever did had nothing to do with a sword.
When Umar ibn al-Khattab became the caliph, he removed Khalid from the command of the armies of Syria,
and put Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah in his place.
The great general became a soldier, under another man's command.
The historians record that Khalid did not argue, and did not leave.
He kept fighting under Abu Ubaydah, as faithfully as when the whole army was his.
And Umar explained why.
The historians record that he said:
I did not remove Khalid out of anger, nor because he betrayed any trust.
But the people were dazzled by him, and I feared they would rely on him, instead of on Allah.
I wanted them to know that it is Allah who gives the victory.
This is what Allah taught the believers, about the help He sent them at Badr:
And Allah made it not but good tidings, and so that your hearts would be assured by it.
And victory is not but from Allah.
Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, and Wise.
Khalid spent his last years in Hims, in Syria.
All his life, he had hoped to die as a martyr on the battlefield.
But Allah decreed otherwise.
The historians record that as he lay on his bed, he said:
I have fought in so many battles, and there is not a hand's span of my body without the mark of a sword, or a spear, or an arrow.
And here I am, dying on my bed.
So may the eyes of cowards never sleep.
Life and death are only in the hand of Allah.
Courage does not shorten a life, and fear does not make it longer.
And the Prophet said:
whoever asks Allah sincerely for martyrdom,
Allah will raise him to the ranks of the martyrs, even if he dies on his bed.
This was reported by Imam Muslim.
What can we learn from the Sword of Allah?
First: no one is too far from Allah.
The man who attacked the believers at Uhud became the man the Prophet called a sword of Allah.
So never give up on anyone, and never give up on yourself.
Second:
Islam gives your gifts a purpose.
Khalid was brave before Islam and after it.
What changed was who he fought for.
Third: true greatness is humble.
When he was removed from command, Khalid did not complain, because he was serving Allah, not his own name.
And fourth: victory is from Allah alone.
The sword was in Khalid's hand, but the help was from Allah.
Allah says about the believers who kept their promise to Him:
Among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah.
Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits his chance.
And they did not change their promise in the least.
May Allah be pleased with Khalid ibn al-Walid, and with all the companions of His Messenger.
And may He give us hearts that are brave for the truth, and humble before Him.
This was the story of Khalid ibn al-Walid, the Sword of Allah.
In sha Allah, more stories of courage, from the prophets and the companions, are coming soon to Quran To You.
Assalamu alaikum.

tagline.en: He stood up for the Prophet when no one else would
tagline.ur: جب کوئی ساتھ نہ تھا، وہ نبی کریم صلی اللہ علیہ وسلم کے ساتھ کھڑے ہوئے

summary.en: The Prophet's uncle and brother through nursing. He stood up to Abu Jahl in front of Quraysh, fought at Badr, and fell at Uhud as the master of the martyrs.
summary.ur: نبی کریم صلی اللہ علیہ وسلم کے چچا اور دودھ شریک بھائی۔ انہوں نے قریش کے سامنے ابو جہل کا مقابلہ کیا، بدر میں لڑے، اور اُحد میں شہیدوں کے سردار بن کر شہید ہوئے۔

cues.text: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome to Stories of the Prophets.
peace and blessings be upon him, and also his brother through nursing.
For years, he did not follow Islam.
Then, in a single afternoon, he walked into the gathering of the leaders of Quraysh,
and stood up for the Messenger of Allah in front of all of them.
His name was Hamzah ibn Abdul-Muttalib.
The believers called him the Lion of Allah, and the Prophet called him the master of the martyrs.
This is his story.
Hamzah was a son of Abdul-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet.
He was only a little older than his nephew Muhammad, and the two of them grew up together in Makkah.
They were also brothers through nursing.
The books of Seerah record that a woman named Thuwaybah nursed them both when they were babies.
Years later, when it was suggested that the Prophet marry the daughter of Hamzah, he said: she is not lawful for me.
She is the daughter of my brother through nursing.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim.
Hamzah grew up to be one of the strongest men of Quraysh.
He loved to hunt, and he was known for his strength and his courage.
People respected him, and few would dare to stand in his way.
When the Prophet began to call people to Allah, Hamzah did not follow him.
But he did not join those who hurt him either.
He kept away, busy with his hunting and his life.
One day, the Prophet was sitting near the hill of as-Safa, when Abu Jahl passed by.
The books of Seerah record that Abu Jahl insulted him, and spoke cruel words against him and against his religion.
The Prophet did not answer.
He stayed silent, and Abu Jahl went off to sit with the leaders of Quraysh near the Kabah.
A woman of Makkah had seen it all.
That evening, Hamzah came back from hunting, with his bow over his shoulder.
It was his habit, before going home, to walk around the Kabah and greet the people sitting there.
But this time, the woman stopped him.
She said: if only you had seen what your nephew Muhammad suffered today from Abu al-Hakam.
He insulted him and hurt him, and Muhammad did not say a word back.
Hamzah's anger rose.
He did not stop to greet anyone.
He walked straight to the gathering where Abu Jahl was sitting,
stood over him, and struck him with his bow, so hard that it wounded his head.
Then he said: do you insult him, when I follow his religion, and say what he says?
Strike me back, if you can.
Men of Abu Jahl's clan jumped up to defend him.
But Abu Jahl said: leave Abu Umarah alone.
By Allah, I did insult his nephew very badly.
Hamzah had spoken in anger, to protect his nephew.
But that night, when he was alone, he began to think about what he had said.
The books of Seerah record that he was troubled.
Leaving the religion of his fathers was no small thing.
He turned to Allah, and asked Him to guide his heart.
The next morning, he went to the Messenger of Allah, who spoke to him about Islam,
and reminded him, until Allah settled faith firmly in his heart.
Hamzah became Muslim, and he never looked back.
Quraysh understood what this meant.
The Prophet now had one of the strongest men of Makkah at his side, and they could no longer hurt him openly as they had before.
Not long after, Umar ibn al-Khattab also became Muslim, and the believers began to feel stronger.
And when the believers emigrated to Madinah, Hamzah emigrated with them,
leaving his home and his wealth behind, for the sake of Allah.
In the second year after the Hijrah, the believers met the army of Quraysh at Badr.
There were a little over three hundred believers, against about a thousand men of Quraysh.
The books of Seerah record that Hamzah fought that day with an ostrich feather fixed on his chest,
so that friend and enemy alike could see where he was in the battle.
Before the armies met, three of the great warriors of Quraysh stepped out in front of their ranks:
Utbah ibn Rabiah, his brother Shaybah, and Utbah's son, al-Walid.
They called out: who will come out to fight us, one against one?
Young men of the Ansar stepped forward.
But Utbah said: we have no need of you.
We want our own people.
So the Messenger of Allah said: stand up, Hamzah.
Stand up, Ali.
Stand up, Ubaydah ibn al-Harith.
Three men of the Prophet's own family walked out.
Hamzah faced Utbah, Ali faced Shaybah, and Ubaydah faced al-Walid.
Hamzah and Ali quickly overcame their opponents.
Ubaydah and al-Walid each wounded the other, so Hamzah and Ali turned to help him, and carried Ubaydah back to the ranks.
This was reported by Imam Abu Dawud.
Ubaydah had been badly wounded.
The books of Seerah record that he died of his wounds a few days later, a martyr, on the way back to Madinah.
Ali ibn Abi Talib later said:
I will be the first to kneel before the Most Merciful, to plead my case, on the Day of Resurrection.
And the companion Abu Dharr used to swear by Allah that an ayah of the Quran was revealed about the six men who met in single combat at Badr:
Hamzah, Ali and Ubaydah, and Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim.
These are two adversaries who have disputed over their Lord.
But those who disbelieved will have cut out for them garments of fire.
Poured upon their heads will be scalding water.
Badr ended in a great victory for the believers, and Hamzah had fought among the bravest of them.
Among the men of Quraysh killed that day was Tuaymah ibn Adi, and it was Hamzah who killed him.
That one blow would follow Hamzah, all the way to the mountain of Uhud.
The man who told the rest of this story was the man who killed Hamzah.
His name was Wahshi.
Many years later, two men visited him in the city of Hims, and asked him to tell them how it had happened.
His account was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Wahshi said:
Hamzah had killed Tuaymah ibn Adi at Badr.
My master, Jubayr ibn Mutim, said to me: if you kill Hamzah in return for my uncle, you are free.
Wahshi was a slave, from Abyssinia.
The books of Seerah record that he was skilled at throwing the spear, in the way of the Abyssinians, and that he rarely missed.
In the third year after the Hijrah, Quraysh marched to Uhud with three thousand men, to take revenge for Badr.
Wahshi went with them.
He had only one aim in that battle.
On the day of Uhud, Hamzah fought like a lion.
Wahshi said: when the armies lined up, a man of Quraysh called Siba came out and called: is there anyone to fight me?
Hamzah went out to him, and said: do you oppose Allah and His Messenger?
Then he attacked him, and Siba fell.
Wahshi said:
I hid behind a rock, waiting for Hamzah.
When he came close to me, I threw my spear at him.
It struck him, and that was his end.
Hamzah ibn Abdul-Muttalib, the Lion of Allah, fell as a martyr at Uhud, in the third year after the Hijrah.
When the battle was over, the Prophet went among the martyrs, and he found his uncle.
The enemy had disfigured the bodies of the fallen, and Hamzah's body had been treated cruelly.
The books of Seerah record that the Prophet's grief that day was greater than anyone had ever seen.
The martyrs of Uhud were buried where they fell, in their clothes and with their blood, without being washed.
The Prophet said:
I will be a witness for these on the Day of Resurrection.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Back in Madinah, the Prophet heard the women of the Ansar weeping for their men who had been killed.
And he said: but Hamzah has no one to weep for him.
So the women came and wept for Hamzah too.
Then the Prophet told them to go home, and not to wail like that for anyone after that day.
This was reported by Imam Ibn Majah.
And the Prophet said: the master of the martyrs is Hamzah ibn Abdul-Muttalib.
This was reported by al-Hakim.
And what became of Wahshi?
He went back to Makkah, and he was given his freedom.
But when Islam spread in Makkah, he left for the city of Taif.
Then the people of Taif sent men to the Prophet to accept Islam, and Wahshi was told: the Prophet does not harm messengers.
So he went with them, and stood before the Messenger of Allah.
Wahshi said: when he saw me, he said: are you Wahshi?
I said: yes.
He said: are you the one who killed Hamzah?
I said: it happened as you have heard.
He said: can you hide your face from me?
So I went away.
Wahshi became Muslim.
As the Prophet taught, Islam wipes away what came before it.
But it was hard for the Prophet to look at the man who had killed his beloved uncle, and so Wahshi kept out of his sight.
Wahshi said: when the Messenger of Allah passed away, and Musaylimah the liar came out, claiming to be a prophet, I said:
I will go out against Musaylimah.
Perhaps I can kill him, and make up for Hamzah.
At the battle of al-Yamamah, Wahshi took the same spear.
He said:
I threw my spear at Musaylimah, and it struck him, and a man of the Ansar struck him with his sword.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
So what can we learn from the Lion of Allah?
First: stand up for what is right.
Hamzah's first step towards Islam was to defend someone who was being wronged, alone, in front of the most powerful men of Makkah.
Second: courage needs guidance.
It was anger that made Hamzah speak that day, but it was faith that made him stay.
He asked Allah to guide him, and Allah guided him.
Third: those who give their lives for Allah are not lost.
Allah says:
And do not say about those who are killed in the way of Allah: they are dead.
Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive it.
And fourth: no one is beyond the mercy of Allah.
Even Wahshi, who killed the Prophet's own uncle, found his way to Islam, and spent his strength against the enemies of the truth.
May Allah be pleased with Hamzah ibn Abdul-Muttalib, the master of the martyrs, and with all the companions of His Messenger.
And may He give us hearts that stand up for the truth.
This was the story of Hamzah ibn Abdul-Muttalib, the Lion of Allah.
In sha Allah, more stories of the prophets and the companions are coming soon to Quran To You.
Assalamu alaikum.

title.en: Bilal, the Voice of the Adhan

summary.en: A slave tortured on the burning sand of Makkah who would only say: One, One. Allah made him the first to call the adhan, and the Prophet heard his footsteps in Paradise.
summary.ur: مکہ کی تپتی ریت پر ستائے جانے والے ایک غلام، جو صرف یہی کہتے رہے: احد، احد۔ اللہ نے انہیں اسلام کا پہلا مؤذن بنایا، اور نبی کریم صلی اللہ علیہ وسلم نے جنت میں ان کے قدموں کی آہٹ سنی۔

cues.text: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome to Stories of the Prophets.
In this episode, the story of one of the companions of our Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
Five times a day, all over the world, a voice rises from the mosques:
Allahu Akbar.
Allah is the Greatest.
And every one of those calls goes back to one man: the first to call the adhan in Islam.
He was once a slave in Makkah, beaten under the burning sun and dragged through its streets.
He was never rich, and he had no tribe to protect him.
And yet, one morning, the Prophet told him:
I heard the sound of your footsteps ahead of me in Paradise.
His name was Bilal ibn Rabah.
This is his story.
Bilal was born a slave, in Makkah.
The books of Seerah record that his father's name was Rabah,
and his mother's name was Hamamah, and that his family came from Abyssinia, across the sea.
He belonged to Umayyah ibn Khalaf, one of the leaders of Quraysh, and one of the bitterest enemies of the new religion.
In Makkah, a slave had no say over his own life.
He worked from morning to night, and he did as he was told.
But when Bilal heard the message of the Prophet, that there is no god but Allah,
that all people are servants of one Lord, and that the most noble of them is the one who fears Him most, his heart answered.
Bilal became one of the very first people to accept Islam.
The companion Abdullah ibn Masud described those early days.
He said: the first to show their Islam openly were seven: the Messenger of Allah,
Abu Bakr, Ammar and his mother Sumayyah, Suhayb, Bilal, and al-Miqdad.
He said:
Allah protected the Messenger through his uncle Abu Talib, and Abu Bakr through his people.
As for the rest, the idol worshippers seized them, dressed them in armour of iron, and left them out in the burning sun.
He said: every one of them, in the end, said with their tongues what the idol worshippers wanted, except Bilal.
His own self meant nothing to him, for the sake of Allah.
So they handed him over to the boys of Makkah, who dragged him through its mountain paths, while he kept saying:
Ahad.
Ahad.
One.
One.
This was reported by Imam Ibn Majah and Imam Ahmad.
The Quran makes clear that whoever is forced to say words of disbelief, while their heart stays firm in faith, is not to blame.
But Bilal would not say them, even with his tongue.
The books of Seerah record what Umayyah ibn Khalaf did to him.
At the hottest hour of the day, he would take Bilal out to the open sand of Makkah,
lay him on his back, and have a great rock placed on his chest.
Then he would say: you will stay like this until you die, or until you deny Muhammad, and worship al-Lat and al-Uzza.
And under that rock, Bilal would only say:
Ahad.
Ahad.
One.
One.
He was not giving a speech.
He was not arguing with them.
With the little breath he had left, he was saying the one truth he would never let go of: that Allah is One.
One day, Abu Bakr as-Siddiq passed by and saw him.
Abu Bakr was a merchant, and he spent his wealth freeing believers who were being tortured.
The books of Seerah record that he bought Bilal from Umayyah, and set him free, for the sake of Allah.
Years later, Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say:
Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master.
By "our master", he meant Bilal.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Many scholars of tafsir say that these ayahs were revealed about Abu Bakr, who freed Bilal, and others like him:
But the righteous one will avoid it: he who gives from his wealth to purify himself,
and not for anyone who has done him a favour, to be repaid, but only seeking the face of his Lord, Most High.
And he is going to be satisfied.
When the believers emigrated to Madinah, Bilal went too.
But the new city had a different air, and many of the emigrants fell ill with fever.
Bilal was one of them.
Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, described how, when the fever left him,
Bilal would raise his voice and recite lines of poetry, longing for the valleys of Makkah, its plants and its springs.
Makkah was the city where he had been tortured, and yet it was still his home.
So the Prophet prayed:
O Allah, make Madinah beloved to us, as You made Makkah beloved to us, or even more.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
In Madinah, the believers built the Prophet's mosque.
But how would they call the people to prayer?
Some suggested a bell, like the Christians.
Others suggested a horn, like the Jews.
Then a companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd saw a dream.
In it, a man taught him the words of the adhan.
He came and told the Prophet, and the Prophet said: it is a true dream, in sha Allah.
Go with Bilal and teach him what you saw, so that he calls it, because his voice is louder than yours.
So Bilal stood and called the adhan.
And when Umar ibn al-Khattab heard it in his house, he came out dragging his cloak,
and said: by the One who sent you with the truth, I saw the same as he saw.
This was reported by Imam Abu Dawud and Imam at-Tirmidhi.
The man who had been dragged through the streets of Makkah, saying One, One, now called the believers to prayer with the words:
I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.
From then on, Bilal called the adhan for the Prophet, and called the iqamah when the prayer was about to begin.
And the Prophet would say to him:
O Bilal, call the iqamah for the prayer, and give us rest by it.
This was reported by Imam Abu Dawud.
For the Prophet, the prayer was not a burden.
It was where he found his rest.
In the second year after the Hijrah, the believers met Quraysh at Badr.
And among the leaders of Quraysh was Umayyah ibn Khalaf, the man who had laid the rock on Bilal's chest.
Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf had been Umayyah's friend before Islam, and on the day of Badr he tried to keep him safe.
But Bilal saw him.
Abdur-Rahman said:
Bilal went to a gathering of the Ansar, and cried out:
Umayyah ibn Khalaf!
May I not be saved, if he is saved!
And Umayyah was killed that day.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
The man who had tortured believers for saying that Allah is One met his end at Badr.
And the slave he had tortured stood among the believers, free.
Six years later, in the eighth year after the Hijrah,
the Prophet entered Makkah with ten thousand believers, and the idols around the Kabah were broken.
The books of Seerah record that the Prophet told Bilal to climb up onto the Kabah, and call the adhan from its roof.
And when the Prophet went inside the Kabah, Bilal was one of the few who went in with him.
Afterwards, the companion Abdullah ibn Umar asked Bilal where the Prophet had prayed inside, and Bilal showed him.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
The same city where Bilal had lain under a rock in the burning sun,
saying One, One, now heard his voice from the top of the House of Allah:
Allahu Akbar.
Allah is the Greatest.
I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.
Allah says:
O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female, and made you peoples and tribes, that you may know one another.
Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.
Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Aware.
And the Prophet said:
O people, your Lord is one, and your father is one.
An Arab has no virtue over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab,
nor a white person over a black person, nor a black person over a white person, except by righteousness.
This was reported by Imam Ahmad.
One morning, at the time of the dawn prayer, the Prophet said to Bilal:
O Bilal, tell me about the deed you have done in Islam that you have the most hope in,
because I heard the sound of your footsteps ahead of me in Paradise.
Bilal said:
I have not done any deed I have more hope in than this: whenever I make wudu,
at any hour of the night or day, I pray with it whatever Allah has written for me to pray.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim.
A small deed, done every day, quietly, for Allah alone.
When the Prophet passed away, a great sadness fell over Madinah.
The historians record that after that, Bilal left Madinah for Syria,
to spend the rest of his life striving in the path of Allah, and that he died there, in Damascus.
The historians also record that as he lay dying, his wife cried out: oh, what sorrow!
And Bilal said: no, what joy!
Tomorrow we will meet the ones we love:
Muhammad and his companions.
So what can we learn from Bilal?
First: faith is not measured by wealth, family or colour.
Bilal had none of the things the world respects, and Allah raised him above the lords of Makkah.
Second: hold on to the truth, even when it costs you.
Under the rock, Bilal had only one word left, and it was the most important word of all:
One.
Third: never look down on a small good deed.
Praying after his wudu took Bilal's footsteps into Paradise.
And fourth:
Allah repays those who help others.
Abu Bakr gave his wealth to free a believer, and Allah promised that he would be satisfied.
May Allah be pleased with Bilal ibn Rabah, and with Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, and with all the companions of His Messenger.
And may He make us among those who answer the call to prayer.
This was the story of Bilal ibn Rabah, the voice of the adhan.
In sha Allah, more stories of the prophets and the companions are coming soon to Quran To You.
Assalamu alaikum.

tagline.en: A small army, a great victory

summary.en: A king chosen by Allah, an army tested at a river, and the few who stayed patient against the mighty Jalut. Then Allah gave Dawud kingship, wisdom and the Zabur.
summary.ur: اللہ کا چُنا ہوا بادشاہ، دریا پر آزمایا گیا لشکر، اور وہ چند صابر لوگ جو طاقتور جالوت کے سامنے ڈٹے رہے۔ پھر اللہ نے داؤد علیہ السلام کو بادشاہی، حکمت اور زبور عطا کی۔

cues.text: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome to Stories of the Prophets.
An army stands on the bank of a river.
The soldiers are tired and thirsty, and the water in front of them is cool and clear.
And their king tells them: whoever drinks from this river is not with me.
Only a few of them obeyed.
And it was those few who went on to face the mighty army of Jalut.
Among them was a man named Dawud.
This is the story of Prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, and of how Allah gives victory to the few who trust Him.
It happened many years after Prophet Musa, peace be upon him.
The Children of Israel had lost their way.
Their enemies had defeated them, driven many of them out of their homes, and taken their children away.
So their leaders went to a prophet who lived among them, and asked him to appoint a king for them, to lead them in battle.
Allah tells us:
Have you not considered the assembly of the Children of Israel after Musa,
when they said to a prophet of theirs: send to us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah?
He said: would you perhaps refrain from fighting, if battle was prescribed for you?
They said: and why should we not fight in the cause of Allah, when we have been driven out from our homes and from our children?
But when battle was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them.
And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
Their prophet knew them well.
He warned them that when the time came to fight, many of them would not keep their word.
And as we will see, he was right.
Allah chose a king for them.
But he was not the man they expected.
And their prophet said to them: indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king.
They said: how can he have kingship over us, while we are more worthy of kingship than him,
and he has not been given any measure of wealth?
He said: indeed, Allah has chosen him over you, and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.
And Allah gives His sovereignty to whom He wills.
And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.
They looked at wealth and family.
But Allah had chosen Talut for the two things that truly matter in a leader: knowledge, and strength.
And Allah gave them a sign, so that their hearts would be at rest:
And their prophet said to them: indeed, a sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you,
in which is assurance from your Lord, and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left, carried by the angels.
Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.
The scholars of tafsir explain that this was a treasured chest of the Children of Israel, which had been taken from them,
and that the angels brought it back to them, as a sign that Talut had truly been chosen by Allah.
So Talut set out with his army.
And on the way, Allah tested them.
And when Talut went forth with the soldiers, he said: indeed, Allah will be testing you with a river.
So whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me,
except one who takes from it in the hollow of his hand.
But they drank from it, except a very few of them.
Then when he had crossed it, along with those who believed with him,
they said: there is no power for us today against Jalut and his soldiers.
But those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: how many a small company has overcome a large company,
by permission of Allah.
And Allah is with the patient.
Think about that test.
It was not a battle.
It was not a sword or a spear.
It was only a drink of water.
But a soldier who cannot hold back from a drink of water for the sake of Allah, how will he hold his ground in front of an army?
Most of them drank.
Only a few held back.
And even among those few, some lost heart when they saw the army of Jalut.
The companion al-Bara ibn Azib said: we, the companions of Muhammad,
used to say that the people of Badr were as many as the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him.
And no one crossed with him except a believer: three hundred and ten, and some more.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Many centuries later, at Badr, Allah would give the same victory, to the same small number of believers.
When the two armies met, the believers who were left did not look at their own numbers.
They turned to Allah.
And when they went forth to face Jalut and his soldiers, they said: our Lord,
pour upon us patience, and plant firmly our feet, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.
So they defeated them by permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut.
And Allah gave him the kingship and wisdom, and taught him from that which He willed.
And if it were not for Allah checking some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted.
But Allah is the possessor of bounty for the worlds.
The Quran does not tell us how Dawud killed Jalut.
Some scholars of tafsir mention, from the reports of the earlier peoples,
that Dawud was then a young man in Talut's army, and that he struck Jalut with a stone from his sling.
Allah knows best.
What the Quran makes clear is that the victory came by the permission of Allah,
and that it came through the few who were patient, and certain that they would meet Him.
After that day, Allah raised Dawud higher and higher.
He made him a king, and a prophet.
And He gave him a book: the Zabur, the Psalms.
And Allah gave Dawud gifts that He did not give to anyone before him.
And We certainly gave Dawud from Us bounty.
We said:
O mountains, repeat Our praises with him, and the birds as well.
And We made iron pliable for him, commanding him: make full coats of armour,
and measure the links precisely, and do righteous deeds.
Indeed I, of what you do, am Seeing.
When Dawud glorified Allah, the mountains and the birds glorified Allah with him.
And iron, the hardest of things, became soft in his hands, so that he could shape it into armour, to protect people in battle.
And yet, this king, who had armies, wealth and power, did not eat from the treasury of his kingdom.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him,
said: no one has ever eaten better food than what he eats from the work of his own hands.
And the Prophet of Allah, Dawud, used to eat from the work of his own hands.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari.
Dawud was also among the most devoted of worshippers.
The Prophet said: the most beloved prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud,
and the most beloved fasting to Allah is the fasting of Dawud.
He would sleep half of the night, then pray for a third of it, then sleep for a sixth of it.
And he would fast one day, and not fast the next.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim.
And Allah gave him a beautiful voice.
When the Prophet heard the beautiful recitation of his companion Abu Musa al-Ashari,
he told him that he had been given a voice like the voices of the family of Dawud.
This was reported by Imam al-Bukhari and Imam Muslim.
So what can we learn from the story of Dawud and Jalut?
First: numbers are not everything.
A small group of believers, patient and certain of meeting Allah, defeated a great army, by His permission.
Second: tests come before victory.
The river came before the battle.
Those who could hold back from what Allah had forbidden were the ones who stood firm when it mattered.
Third: when you face something bigger than you, turn to Allah.
The believers did not boast.
They asked Him for patience, for firm feet, and for victory.
And fourth: true greatness is humble.
Dawud became a king and a prophet, and still he ate from the work of his own hands, and spent his nights in prayer.
May Allah make us among the patient, the few who trust Him.
And may He plant our feet firmly on the truth.
This was the story of Prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, and Jalut.
